name: Simony and the campaign against it
plain_explanation: Simony -- the buying and selling of ecclesiastical offices -- was rampant in the tenth and early eleventh centuries: kings sold bishoprics, bishops in turn sold lesser preferments. Reformers attacked this not only as sinful but because it made appointment depend on wealth rather than merit, tied bishops to secular rulers who had sold them their offices, and gave newly appointed clergy strong incentive to recoup their investment through worldly rather than spiritual pursuits.
precise_definition: The sale or purchase of ecclesiastical office or sacraments, condemned by eleventh-century reformers as both a moral sin and a structural cause of episcopal subservience to secular power and of clerical worldliness.
why_it_mattered: The campaign against simony was inseparable from the political struggle for clerical independence from lay control, since ending the sale of bishoprics by kings directly undercut royal power over Church appointments.
historical_origin: Widespread throughout the tenth and early eleventh centuries; documented by Peter Damian's 1059 discovery that every cleric in Milan, from the archbishop down, was guilty of it.
examples: Gerbert's (Pope Sylvester II's) satirical description of bishops boasting of recouping the gold they paid for office by selling ordinations in turn
Nicholas II's 1059 decree invalidating future ordinations performed by simoniac clergy (not made retroactive, to avoid invalidating most existing ordinations)
influence_on_later_thinkers: Continued to be a central concern of later medieval and Reformation-era Church reform movements.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly political: ending simony meant ending royal control over episcopal appointments, feeding directly into the investiture conflict.
